Dante Alighieri. An Italian poet and philosopher from twelve sixty-five to thirteen twenty-one whose Divine Comedy is one of the greatest works of world literature. Writing in the vernacular Florentine Italian rather than Latin, Dante created an epic synthesis of medieval theology, classical learning, and personal allegory that established Italian literature as a major European force and anticipated the Renaissance humanist turn.

Dante was born and active in Florence during a period of intense political and factional strife. His support for the Guelph faction led to his exile in thirteen two—a trauma that shaped his vision of spiritual pilgrimage and political justice. The Divine Comedy, completed around thirteen twenty, is an epic poem recounting Dante's journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, guided by the Roman poet Virgil and finally by his beloved Beatrice.

By writing in Italian vernacular rather than Latin, Dante demonstrated that non-Latin languages could express sophisticated theological and philosophical ideas. He thereby opened literature to broader audiences and vindicated the vernacular as a vehicle for high culture. The Divine Comedy synthesizes medieval theology, especially Aquinas, classical literature including Virgil, Ovid, and Homer, contemporary politics, and personal experience into a cosmic allegory. The journey parallels both Christian salvation and Dante's own intellectual development.

Dante's portrayal of Hell and its punishments—suffering proportional to sin—became culturally dominant. His vivid depictions of historical and mythological figures reshaped how Europeans understood those figures. The poem anticipates Renaissance humanism by integrating pagan classical literature with Christian theology rather than treating them as opposed. It also foregrounds individual human experience and psychology.

Dante's other works were influential in literary theory and the valorization of Italian as a serious language. La Vita Nuova is an earlier poetic romance. Convivio presents philosophical essays. De Vulgari Eloquentia treats the vernacular language itself.

The Divine Comedy is Dante's masterwork and one of literature's greatest achievements. The Italian Renaissance was founded on Dante's pioneering of vernacular Italian literature. Florence is his native city, whose politics exiled him and shaped his vision. Dante synthesized medieval theology and philosophy into literature itself. The Divine Comedy is written in vernacular Italian, not Latin. Poetry, and epic poetry specifically, is the form Dante chose for his greatest work. Medieval philosophy, drawing on Aquinas and Aristotle and scholastic thought, permeates the work. Dante anticipated Renaissance humanism by integrating classical and Christian traditions.
